I am a new revert to Islam. This was of the first Masjids I visited for Jummah prayer. I was nervous but a lot of warm faces welcomed me and gave me Salams on the way in.

The Khutba was on the Hadith of what we say in congregational prayers when we are in groups. It was almost like it was speaking to me directly as it was my first time.

Afterwards some of the gentlemen and the Imam himself invited me in the back to sit and have some Rice Pudding. It was delicious!

I spoke to the other brothers and we talked about what brought me to Texas and to Islam. One of them actually used to work near my hometown in California.

This was about a year ago. I’ve been back several times if I’m in Conroe or N. Spring on a Friday this is my Go-to Masjid.

I came to the masjid, for Friday prayer this my second time coming since closer to my home  and an announcement was made asking people to move my school bus  There was no problem—I immediately went to move my bus.

As I was already moving it, a man came up to me in a very rude manner and insisted that I needed to move my bus “right now.” He was looking directly at me and speaking disrespectfully, even though he could clearly see I was already leaving there was nothing wrong he’s car could fit  Instead of arguing, I simply continued moving my vehicle.

He claimed it was an emergency, but his behavior didn’t reflect that—he seemed completely relaxed, casually sipping his coffee. My issue isn’t with being asked to move my bus. It’s with the unnecessary disrespect. If he saw I was already complying, there was no need to approach me that way . A polite tone—or simply saying nothing at all—would have been more appropriate.

I hope everyone who visits the masjid, especially women, is treated with the respect and kindness that Islam teaches.

reviews.text:
السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته،

أكتب إليكم بكل احترام لألفت انتباهكم إلى مشكلة واجهتها مرتين أثناء حضوري إلى المسجد.

في كلتا المرتين، صليت في مصلى الأخوات. وبعد أن توضأت ودخلت قاعة الصلاة، كان أول ما لاحظته هو أن الجو كان شديد الحرارة والرطوبة. بدأت بالتعرق فورًا، وكانت درجة الحرارة غير مريحة إلى حد جعل من الصعب عليّ التركيز والحفاظ على خشوعي وصلتي بالله أثناء الصلاة.

في المرة الأولى، توجهت إلى جهاز تنظيم الحرارة وخفضت درجة الحرارة، لأنني شعرت بصدق أنني لن أتمكن من الصلاة براحة otherwise. وعندما عدت في اليوم التالي، لاحظت أن جهاز تنظيم الحرارة قد وُضع داخل صندوق شفاف مقفل، مما منع أي شخص من تعديل درجة الحرارة. وكانت القاعة مرة أخرى في حدود 80 درجة فهرنهايت، وشديدة الحرارة للغاية.

أتفهم أن الحفاظ على درجة حرارة مريحة في جميع أنحاء مسجد كبير قد يكون أمرًا صعبًا، وأنا لا أطلب معاملة خاصة. ومع ذلك، أؤمن بأن راحة الأخوات واحتياجاتهن ينبغي أن تحظى بالاهتمام نفسه الذي تحظى به راحة الإخوة واحتياجاتهم.

فنحن كنساء مسلمات مأمورات بالحجاب والبقاء مستورات أثناء وجودنا في المسجد. وارتداء الملابس الساترة بالكامل في مكان للصلاة حار ورطب أصلًا قد يجعل الظروف غير مريحة بشكل خاص. ولا ينبغي أن نضطر إلى الاختيار بين تحمل الحرارة الشديدة وعدم القدرة على التركيز في الصلاة كما ينبغي.

المسجد بيت الله، ويستحق كل من الإخوة والأخوات في الأمة أن يشعروا بالاحترام والاهتمام وتوفير الظروف المناسبة لهم عندما يأتون للعبادة. وأرجو بصدق من إدارة المسجد إعادة النظر في درجة الحرارة في مصلى الأخوات، والتفكير في حل يتيح بقاء جانبي المسجد في درجة حرارة مريحة ومعقولة.

أطرح هذا الأمر لأنني أهتم بالمسجد وأرغب في أن يكون مكانًا مرحبًا بجميع المسلمين. كما أؤمن بأن من أُوكلت إليهم مسؤولية القيادة سيُسألون في نهاية المطاف أمام الله عن كيفية معاملتهم لمن يأتون إلى بيته.

نسأل الله أن يهدينا جميعًا، ويزيدنا فهمًا، ويجعل مساجدنا أماكن يستطيع فيها كل مؤمن أن يعبده بطمأنينة وراحة.

جزاكم الله خيرًا على تخصيص وقتكم للنظر في هذا الأمر.

والسلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته.
reviews.textTranslated:
Peace, mercy, and blessings of God be upon you.

I am writing to you respectfully to bring to your attention a problem I encountered twice while attending the mosque.

On both occasions, I prayed in the women's prayer area. After performing ablution and entering the prayer hall, the first thing I noticed was that it was extremely hot and humid. I immediately began to sweat, and the temperature was so uncomfortable that it made it difficult for me to concentrate and maintain my focus and connection with God during prayer.

The first time, I went to the thermostat and lowered the temperature, as I genuinely felt I wouldn't be able to pray comfortably otherwise. When I returned the following day, I noticed that the thermostat had been placed inside a locked, transparent box, preventing anyone from adjusting the temperature. The hall was again around 80 degrees Fahrenheit, which is unbearably hot.

I understand that maintaining a comfortable temperature throughout a large mosque can be challenging, and I am not asking for special treatment. However, I believe that the comfort and needs of the women should receive the same attention as those of the men.

As Muslim women, we are commanded to wear the hijab and remain covered while in the mosque. Wearing full-covering clothing in a place of prayer that is already hot and humid can make conditions particularly uncomfortable. We should not have to choose between enduring the intense heat and being unable to concentrate properly during prayer.

The mosque is the house of God, and all brothers and sisters in the community deserve to feel respected, cared for, and provided with suitable conditions when they come to worship. I sincerely request that the mosque administration reconsider the temperature in the women's prayer area and find a solution that allows both sides of the mosque to remain at a comfortable and reasonable temperature.

I raise this issue because I care about the mosque and want it to be a welcoming place for all Muslims. I also believe that those entrusted with leadership will ultimately be held accountable before God for how they treat those who come to His house.

We ask God to guide us all, increase our understanding, and make our mosques places where every believer can worship Him in peace and comfort.

May God reward you for taking the time to consider this matter. Peace, mercy, and blessings of God be upon you.

I have been going to ISRA for Tuesday majlises (gatherings) and other meetings for years. I also went to umrah with ISRA in 2023. I always feel welcome here and it is one of the very few places where I feel I belong.

These days I am taking Tafseer Intensive classes from Mufti Wasim. These weekend classes are what I was dreaming for. Mufti Wasim is a blessing for this community. It is like a Qur’an feast and I look forward to the weekends with great excitement to study tafseer with his guidance.

Today while studying the duas in several places in the surah Al-i Imran I wanted to memorize everything Quran. Every letter, every word of it.

May Allah bless Mufti and all ISRA team and give them success for their service to the youth and Muslim community in general. Ameen.

reviews.name: Karimah Pheasant
reviews.text:
We moved from out of state, and one of the greatest blessings Allah granted our family was finding ISRA. From the moment we arrived, we felt welcomed, valued, and embraced by a community that truly embodies the spirit of Islam.
Our children participated in the after school Maktab program and benefited tremendously. They memorized many short surahs and duas. They looked forward to every class with excitement. What stood out most was how learning was made engaging and meaningful through interactive activities, games, and lessons that nurtured both knowledge and character. As parents, there is no greater joy than seeing your children eager to learn about their deen.
The staff is incredibly caring, dedicated, and sincere in their service. They go above and beyond to make everyone feel supported, and it genuinely feels like being part of an extended family. The warmth, kindness, and sense of belonging we experienced at ISRA is rare and deeply appreciated.
Mufti MWK is a true blessing to the community. His depth of knowledge is matched by his humility, wisdom, and approachable nature. He has cultivated a welcoming environment where people feel comfortable seeking knowledge, asking questions, and strengthening their connection with Allah. The positive impact of his leadership is evident in every aspect of the community he has helped build. We are immensely grateful for everything this community has done for our family and pray that many others are able to benefit from it as we have.
May Allah SWT preserve and protect ISRA, place abundant barakah in its work, and make it a means of guidance for generations to come. May Allah reward Mufti MWK, the imam, the teachers, staff, volunteers, and every person who serves this community with sincerity. Ameen.

I understand that security has a job to do and sometimes they need to be firm with people so everyone follows the rules, but this particular situation was completely unnecessary. My father is older and still drives. He accidentally turned into the school parking area, and there was no way for him to safely back out unless we pulled in and reversed.

We tried explaining to the security guard that it was simply a mistake, but instead of understanding the situation, he came over yelling, taking pictures of our car, and speaking to us extremely rudely.

I was very disappointed by my experience. This was my second Jumu’ah at this mosque, and the entire khutbah was delivered in Arabic. While there is a QR code for a live English translation, it is not practical to follow a translation on a phone during the sermon.

The House of Allah should welcome and serve the entire Muslim community, not be confined to only one language group. In a diverse country like the United States, many Muslims do not understand Arabic and are unable to benefit from the khutbah.

Because of this, I would not recommend this mosque to anyone who does not understand Arabic. I sincerely hope the mosque will consider delivering the khutbah in English or at least providing a spoken English summary so that everyone can understand the message.

I’m very disappointed with my experience with Masjid Al Hedayah. From what I witnessed and experienced, I felt that the way the imam was treated and removed was unfair and poorly handled.

I also have serious concerns about how charity and community funds are prioritized. In my view, money and resources were spent on things such as painting the basketball court red, while there seemed to be much less willingness to invest in the Islamic school and the education of the children in the community. When a community is asking people to donate, I believe there should be greater transparency about how those donations are being prioritized and whether they are actually going toward the needs that matter most.

I’m also concerned about how fairly people are treated within the community. There have been situations involving another imam where I felt the treatment came across as discriminatory and deeply concerning.

A masjid should be built on justice, good character, transparency, education, and equal treatment for everyone. Unfortunately, my experience has left me feeling that Masjid Al Hedayah has fallen short of those standards. I hope the leadership takes these concerns seriously and works toward creating a more welcoming, fair, transparent, and united community.

However, there are a few serious concerns regarding the prayer leaders when Sheikh Sayed is away:

Sunnah Standards: At times, individuals leading the prayer lack standard Islamic attire—such as not having a beard, not wearing a kufi, or wearing garments that hang below the ankles. This sets an improper example for the community regarding the Sunnah.

Qualified Imams: There are instances where young boys or individuals without proper attire and appearance are assigned to lead prayers like Asr, even when qualified adult community members are present.

Leading Salah is a significant responsibility and should be handled with care. I urge the management and ISGH to address these matters and ensure proper guidelines are followed according to recognized scholarly standards.

reviews.text:
1-Star Review

I am extremely disappointed and honestly hurt by the way I was treated when I came to this masjid simply trying to pray Dhuhr.

I walked up to the masjid and greeted the man standing outside by saying, “As-salamu alaykum.” I explained that I was trying to enter through the women’s side and asked him how I could get in. He told me that there was a women’s section but that “they’re not praying right now.” At the time, I only had about 14 minutes left to pray Dhuhr, so I explained that I needed somewhere to pray.

I then asked if I could enter through the men’s side just to pray, and he refused. Instead, he asked me, “Can’t you just go home and pray?” I explained that I was working and could not simply go home because I was doing door-to-door sales in the area I don’t currently have a car and my house is 30 minutes away from here.

He still refused to let me into the masjid.

I told him that if I could not pray inside, I would simply pray outside. He then asked me, “Can’t you just go somewhere else?” It was raining, and I was standing under the awning of the masjid, so I asked why I would need to leave when there was a masjid right there where I could pray.

When I explained that it was raining and I was already at the masjid, he responded, “I don’t think that looks good.” He then went inside and locked the door behind him, leaving me outside.

I was not asking to disturb anyone, enter a restricted area, or do anything inappropriate. I was simply a Muslim woman trying to fulfill my obligation to pray before the prayer time ended.

What makes this experience even more upsetting is that, from what I understand, this masjid was founded by Saeeda Khan, a woman. It is incredibly disappointing to be turned away from a masjid when I was only seeking a place to worship Allah especially considering how excited I was to see that I was near a masjid as I’m working.

A masjid should be a place where Muslims feel welcomed, especially when they are actively trying to pray. I understand that there may be rules regarding access to different prayer areas, but there should be a compassionate and reasonable way to accommodate someone who is trying to pray and has very little time remaining.

This experience left me feeling unwelcome, embarrassed, and deeply disappointed. I sincerely hope the leadership addresses how women who come to the masjid to pray are treated and makes sure that no one else is made to feel the way I was made to feel.

Because of this experience, I will never attend a service at this masjid. Allah did not teach us to lack compassion and empathy and he would not condone such behavior.

Tajweed Institute has truly become a second home for so many of us. The diversity of the community is one of the most beautiful parts of this masjid. People from all backgrounds come together with love, respect, and sincerity, creating an atmosphere that feels warm and welcoming from the moment you walk through the doors.

The staff and volunteers are always incredibly kind, organized, and helpful. You can genuinely feel how much they care about the community and the experience of everyone who attends. They offer many programs for sisters each month, which is a plus.

The khutbahs by Dr. Ra’ed are always relevant, beneficial, and deeply impactful. They address real life struggles and reminders in a way that connects with people of all ages and backgrounds. And the recitation of Sheikh, is truly beautiful, MashaAllah. It brings peace and tranquility to the heart every single time.

One thing that also stands out is how clean and well maintained the facility always is. The masjid is cared for with excellence and respect.

Overall, Tajweed Institute is honestly the best masajid in Houston. A place filled with knowledge, community, sincerity, and warmth. May Allah continue to bless everyone who helps make it what it is. Ameen.

Masha'Allah, a large and well-organized mosque.

First, you should know that those in charge of the mosque are Sufis. I prayed with them on Friday and only noticed a supplication shortly after the prayer.

I prayed on Friday, September 25th, and the prayer was as follows: The time for Dhuhr prayer began at 1:15 PM.

At the same time, they called the Adhan (call to prayer).

After a quarter of an hour (1:30 PM), a man spoke in English for twenty minutes. Then they all stood up (I thought it was the Iqamah), but they stood up and performed four Rak'ahs (units of prayer) and two Taslims (greetings of peace). Then the Imam ascended the pulpit and began the two sermons (two minutes each, consisting of supplications in Arabic and praise of the Prophet and his Companions).

Then he called the Iqamah…

Another observation regarding the Iqamah, specifically the two Hayya 'ala as-Salahs (Come to prayer, come to prayer…), is that they were repeated twice.

Marriage in Islam is meant to be simple and accessible, not something that creates a significant financial burden. I completely understand having reasonable administrative requirements, but these fees seem unnecessarily high. I hope the mosque will reconsider its approach and focus more on making nikah accessible to the community rather than placing financial barriers on it.

I am a Christian, and I want to be completely candid about where I stand theologically.

I respect Muslims as human beings made in the image of God, and I have no hatred toward anyone because they are Muslim. But respect for people does not require compromise concerning truth.

I cannot affirm or endorse Islamic theology because Islam fundamentally contradicts the historic Christian Gospel concerning the identity and saving work of Jesus Christ.

The Bible teaches that Jesus Christ is not merely a prophet. He is the eternal Son of God who became flesh.

John 1:1 says, “the Word was God,” and John 1:14 declares that “the Word was made flesh.”

Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man.

He was crucified for sinners.

He physically rose from the dead.

He ascended into heaven.

And He will return in glory to judge the living and the dead.

Islam rejects central claims of this Gospel, including Christ's divine Sonship and the Christian confession concerning His crucifixion and resurrection.

That is not a minor denominational disagreement.

That is a fundamental contradiction concerning who Jesus Christ is and how sinners are reconciled to God.

The apostle Paul gave an uncompromising warning:

«“Though that we, or an Angel from heaven, preach unto you another Gospel than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.”
— Galatians 1:8»

The Christian Gospel is not that mankind earns salvation through religious works or human righteousness.

Salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith, and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8

And Jesus Christ Himself declared:

«“I am the way, and the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father but by me.”
— John 14:6»

Therefore, I will not say that Islam and Christianity are simply two different paths to the same God.

They are not.

I will love my Muslim neighbors.
I will treat them with dignity.
I will speak to them respectfully.
I will gladly have honest conversations with them.

But I will not compromise the deity of Christ, His death and bodily resurrection, the Trinity, the authority of Scripture, or salvation through Christ alone in order to manufacture religious harmony.

Christians are commanded to speak the truth in love—not to abandon truth in the name of tolerance.

So my position is simple:

I reject Islam's theology because I believe it contradicts the revealed Gospel of Jesus Christ.

And I say that not because I hate Muslims, but because I believe the Gospel is true and because I genuinely want Muslims to know the real Jesus Christ revealed in Scripture.

Jesus Christ is Lord.

“There is salvation in no other.” — Acts 4:12
